Meeting header: 2025-07-22 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~46 mins | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Sarah (Pinebridge), Tom (Pinebridge), Evan (Pinebridge)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE. With me is Priya, our solutions engineer. Today we'll do a quick hosted API demo focused on chat/text gen basics — streaming, key generation params, and retry strategies. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Sarah (Pinebridge): Good, thanks. We're excited — trying to get a pilot running for an in-product assistant. Key constraints: sub-200ms median latency for short prompts, logging / audit for compliance, and SSO.
[00:16] Alex: Perfect, those are common. Priya, do you want to take us through the console + API flow?
[00:20] Priya (Redwood SE): Sure. I'll share my screen — give me a sec. (screen shares) Alright, starting with the Console overview — this is the hosted API side. We have the model selection, request monitoring, and a place to configure streaming. For quick context — streaming is Server-Sent Events (SSE) for tokens, you can consume partial tokens as they arrive.
[00:40] Priya: Two quick notes before we call out code: 1) The SDK and REST endpoints both support streaming, 2) we expose request-level metadata in the response headers for tracing.
[00:52] Tom (Platform Eng): Is the streaming format compatible with typical EventSource handlers in the browser?
[00:56] Priya: Yes. It's plain SSE so EventSource or any SSE client works. For Node, we often recommend an SSE parser like eventsource or a raw fetch with text streaming.
[01:08] Evan (PM): Can you show an example of a streaming call?
[01:10] Priya: Absolutely, here's a curl example — note this is simplified: curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"model":"redwood-alpha-chat","stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Summarize our product"}]}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat/stream
[01:30] Priya: You'd see SSE events with data chunks like event: token
data: {"text":"We build..."}

[01:36] Sarah: Nice. How do we handle partial outputs if we need to index or persist them? We don't want to store user PII mid-stream.
[01:44] Priya: Good question. Common pattern: buffer client-side until you reach a non-sensitive checkpoint or until final event. On the server side, Redwood offers response hooks — webhooks for completed responses; you can opt to only get the final result to your backend. Also in Console you can turn off logs for certain endpoints for compliance.
[01:58] Alex: Also worth pointing out connection resilience — the client should implement an exponential backoff and resume logic. If you're using idempotency keys you can safely re-issue requests; for streaming specifically we recommend chunk checkpoints with a conversation position token.
[02:12] Tom: Conversation position token? Can you explain a bit?
[02:14] Priya: Sure — it's a lightweight opaque token we return with each response that encodes the conversation state on the server. If a connection drops, you can reconnect and pass that token to resume from the last committed state rather than re-sending entire context. It's optional but helpful for long chats.
[02:30] Evan: Is that part of the hosted API today or a roadmap item?
[02:33] Priya: We have a resume token feature on hosted for certain plans; I'll confirm available tiers after.
[02:39] Sarah: Ok. Let's talk params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens — defaults and recommended values for user-facing chat?
[02:46] Priya: For a user-facing assistant where determinism matters, we often recommend temperature 0.0-0.3 and top_p disabled or around 0.8. For discovery features you might bump to 0.7. max_tokens usually depends on expected reply length — for short replies 64-256. Also the Redwood API exposes response_sampling in the console for A/B testing.
[03:08] Alex: And don't forget beam_search or deterministic sampling isn't always supported on all model variants — we expose which sampling modes are available per model in the model catalog.
[03:18] [03:18] Sarah: For latency concerns, what are the tradeoffs when increasing max_tokens or higher temperature?
[03:24] Priya: Higher max_tokens obviously increases per-request compute time and cost. Temperature affects sampling randomness but not compute. The effective latency impact is mostly from sequence length and model size. For shorter median latencies, prefer smaller model family or quantized variants; Redwood's runtime selects kernels to optimize for that.
[03:40] Tom: For the pilot we want to keep costs predictable. Is there a way to cap per-user spend or throttle token usage?
[03:47] Alex: Yes — usage quotas per API key, per-route limits, and rate-limiting are supported. You can also set token budgets and reject requests once exceeded. Priya can show quotas in Console.
[03:58] Priya: (navigates) Here — per-route rate limits, token quotas, and burst policies. You can also set custom error messages when quotas are hit.
[04:10] Evan: Back to retries — what's your recommended retry strategy for 5xx vs 429?
[04:15] Priya: For 5xx transient errors, exponential backoff with jitter is standard. For 429 (rate limit), honor Retry-After header; use linear or exponential backoff and consider circuit-breaker logic to stop immediate retries. For streaming, if you see a mid-stream 5xx you should reconnect and resume if using the resume token; if that's not available, best to re-issue with idempotency key and dedupe on final result.
[04:39] Tom: How do idempotency keys interact with streaming? If you re-issue, will you get partial tokens duplicate?
[04:44] Priya: Idempotency keys are applied to the final generation result on the server side. If a request fails before completion, re-issuing with the same key will either resume or return the same final output once available. For partial tokens, you'll need client-side dedupe when appending chunks — we include chunk sequence numbers in SSE events to help with de-duplication.
[05:02] Sarah: Are there SDK helpers that wrap this for us? We're building in React + Node.
[05:06] Priya: Yes — our JS SDK has a streaming helper that handles reconnects, dedupe, and exposes an onToken callback. We'll share sample code. Example: const stream = client.chat.stream({ messages, onToken: t => append(t) }); stream.start();
[05:22] Alex: Quick qualification — Sarah, you mentioned SSO earlier. Are you using Okta?
[05:26] Sarah: Yeah, Okta SAML SSO and we need SCIM provisioning ideally.
[05:31] Alex: Redwood supports SSO via SAML and OIDC, and we have SCIM for user provisioning on enterprise plans. We'll include the security pack link.
[05:39] Tom: What about encryption in transit and at rest? KMS?
[05:42] Priya: TLS in transit by default. For at-rest encryption and customer-managed keys we offer KMS integrations for Private/Dedicated deployments. For hosted we have managed KMS but can do bring-your-own-key on enterprise.
[05:55] Evan: Any compliance attestations?
[05:57] Alex: SOC 2 Type II and in progress for ISO 27001 at the time of conversation; we'll attach the compliance pack.
[06:06] [06:06] Priya: Back to demo — I want to show a short end-to-end flow. I'll use the JS SDK in a Node sample. (types) Ok, creating client with API key, then client.chat.create with messages, with stream=false to show non-streamed, then stream=true for streaming.
[06:28] Priya: Non-stream call response arrives as JSON with choices array and a finish_reason. For the streaming example you'll see multiple token events and a final 'done' event.
[06:36] Priya: I'll deliberately set temperature to 0.2 and max_tokens 120 to mimic your short assistant.
[06:42] [06:42] (Slight audio glitch)
[06:45] Sarah: Sorry, bit of packet loss here.
[06:46] Alex: No worries.
[06:48] Priya: Continuing — here's a snippet of streaming output in the console window. (reads) token #1: "Hi" token #2: "there," token #3: "I" token #4: "can"... you'll see it flush progressively.
[07:03] Tom: In your console, is there an option to capture latency percentiles per API key? We need P50/P95 dashboards.
[07:10] Priya: Yes — per-key and per-route latency breakdown, plus token-level cost. You can create dashboards and alerts for anomalies like sudden P95 spikes.
[07:20] Evan: On the subject of cost, do you have guidance or an Optimize tool to recommend batching or caching strategies?
[07:26] Priya: Redwood Optimize does exactly that — based on call patterns we'll suggest batching windows, cache TTLs for prefix caching, and recommend smaller model variants or quantization profiles for your workload. For chat, prefix caching (for repeated system prompts) often saves a lot.
[07:40] Sarah: Oh — can you explain prefix caching?
[07:43] Priya: Sure — if you have a long system or assistant prompt that's the same across users, we can cache the KV cache for that prefix on the server so subsequent requests only compute tokens for the new user messages. That reduces effective compute and latency.
[07:55] Tom: Is prefix caching available on hosted?
[07:58] Priya: Yes, hosted has prefix caching; Dedicated and Private expose more configuration knobs for cache warmup and persistence.
[08:05] Sarah: For the pilot we may need to redact or not retain logs. How granular is log retention?
[08:10] Priya: Per-route logging toggles and retention windows are available. You can opt to disable full request body logging and only retain metadata like request_id and timestamp, which helps with audits without storing user content.
[08:22] [08:22] Alex: Let's switch to an edge case: sudden rate limit flood — how would Redwood recommend protecting downstream services?
[08:29] Priya: Implement a token bucket on your side to smooth the bursts, and Redwood's rate-limit headers will help adapt. On our side we provide backpressure signals and client libraries implement recommended retry strategies. For larger customers we can provision dedicated capacity to avoid noisy neighbors.
[08:45] Tom: That raises a question: our compliance team might push for Dedicated given audit needs. For the pilot though, hosted is easier. Any migration path differences?
[08:54] Priya: The API surface is the same for hosted and Dedicated, and we support model version pinning so migrations are mostly configuration changes. Dedicated offers VPC peering and private endpoints. We'll document migration steps.
[09:07] Evan: Can you run a quick test showing token cost for a 200-token reply from a 4k-window model?
[09:12] Priya: Sure, in Console we have an estimator — for model X it's approx 200 tokens * X price = $0.YZ (example). I'll attach detailed price sheet. But remember embedding costs differ.
[09:26] Sarah: On pricing, do you have committed usage tiers?
[09:29] Alex: Yes, we offer committed reserved capacity for Dedicated and discounts for committed usage on hosted. Details in pricing doc.
[09:35] [09:35] Priya: Quick demo of error handling in code: try/catch around stream events, listening for 'error' events, implementing a retry with exponential backoff: wait = base * 2^attempt + jitter, cap at 30s and abort after 5 attempts. For 429, respect Retry-After header.
[09:54] Tom: Do you version API and how are breaking changes handled?
[09:58] Alex: API versioning is explicit — we support v1, v2 etc. Breaking changes are rolled out with deprecation windows and a console notice; for big changes we run canary and customer notifications.
[10:09] Sarah: Ok. We're close to time. Want to surface some follow-ups so priorities are clear: 1) security pack and compliance artifacts, 2) quickstart + sample code for streaming/resume + dedupe, 3) tailored benchmark for our expected 2k token full-chat with 200 concurrent users, 4) pricing for pilot — estimate monthly.
[10:28] Alex: Got it, we'll own 1-3 and get a preliminary pricing estimate. Any other blockers?
[10:34] Sarah: Data residency — can you store logs in EU region only?
[10:38] Priya: Hosted has regional endpoints; you can pin to eu-west region. For strict data residency we recommend Dedicated or Private deployment.
[10:47] Evan: One last technical thing — what's the recommended pattern for streaming to mobile clients with flaky networks?
[10:51] Priya: For mobile, send short incremental chunks and use resume tokens. Also implement client-side acknowledgements so servers know which chunks were received; if not received, server can replay missing sequence numbers. Smaller chunk sizes help.
[11:05] (Cross-talk)
[11:07] Alex: Alright, quick recap — we'll send the quickstart and sample code, Priya will run benchmarks, and we'll include security docs and pricing. Sarah to confirm pilot scope and stakeholder list.
[11:18] Sarah: Sounds good. Thanks for the demo.
[11:20] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email and I'll drop the links.
